     6	  // call routing + callee/arg evaluation (#callee/#args/#argCont) live in call.k;
     7	  // this module owns the frame lifecycle (bind params, return, pop).
     8	  syntax KItem ::= frame(continuation: K, callerEnv: Int, savedLoc: Int)
     9	                 | #bindP(ParamNames, Vals)
    10	                 | "#pop"
    11	                 | "#endcall"
    12	
    13	  // ==== def / anonymous closure =============================================
    14	  rule <k> FuncDef(F:String, Params(PNS:ParamNames), BODY:Stmts) => .K ... </k>
    15	       <env> L:Int </env>
    16	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ F <- closureVal(PNS, BODY, L) ], _) ... </scopes>
    17	
    18	  syntax Expr ::= closureExpr(ParamNames, Stmts)
    19	  rule <k> closureExpr(PNS:ParamNames, BODY:Stmts) => closureVal(PNS, BODY, L) ... </k>
    20	       <env> L:Int </env>
    21	
    22	  // ==== annotated def/lambda (closure cells; spec 2.3) ======================
    23	  // closureValC(params, cellvars, body, captured-cells). No frame anchor: all
    24	  // enclosing-local reads are freevars (symtable-complete) and go through the
    25	  // captured cells; everything else is global/builtin, so the callee frame's
    26	  // parent is the module scope (0) — sound after the defining frame dies.
    27	  syntax Val ::= closureValC(ParamNames, ParamNames, Stmts, Map)
    28	
    29	  // capture: resolve each freevar to the enclosing frame's cellRef, then bind
    30	  // (FuncDef) or yield (Lambda) the closure value.
    31	  syntax KItem ::= #mkClosure(String, ParamNames, ParamNames, ParamNames, Stmts, Map)
    32	                 | #mkLambda(ParamNames, ParamNames, ParamNames, Stmts, Map)
    33	  rule <k> FuncDef(F:String, Params(PNS:ParamNames), CellVars(CVS:ParamNames),
    34	                   FreeVars(FVS:ParamNames), BODY:Stmts)
    35	        => #mkClosure(F, PNS, CVS, FVS, BODY, .Map) ... </k>
    36	  rule <k> #mkClosure(F:String, PNS:ParamNames, CVS:ParamNames,
    37	                      (FV:String, FVR:ParamNames), BODY:Stmts, CM:Map)
    38	        => #mkClosure(F, PNS, CVS, FVR, BODY, CM [ FV <- {M[FV]}:>Val ]) ... </k>
    39	       <env> L:Int </env>
    40	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    41	       requires FV in_keys(M)
    42	  rule <k> #mkClosure(F:String, PNS:ParamNames, CVS:ParamNames,
    43	                      .ParamNames, BODY:Stmts, CM:Map) => .K ... </k>
    44	       <env> L:Int </env>
    45	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ F <- closureValC(PNS, CVS, BODY, CM) ], _) ... </scopes>
    46	
    47	  rule <k> Lambda(Params(PNS:ParamNames), E:Expr)
    48	        => closureVal(PNS, Return(E) .Stmts, L) ... </k>
    49	       <env> L:Int </env>
    50	  rule <k> Lambda(Params(PNS:ParamNames), CellVars(CVS:ParamNames),
    51	                  FreeVars(FVS:ParamNames), E:Expr)
    52	        => #mkLambda(PNS, CVS, FVS, Return(E) .Stmts, .Map) ... </k>
    53	  rule <k> #mkLambda(PNS:ParamNames, CVS:ParamNames,
    54	                     (FV:String, FVR:ParamNames), BODY:Stmts, CM:Map)
    55	        => #mkLambda(PNS, CVS, FVR, BODY, CM [ FV <- {M[FV]}:>Val ]) ... </k>
    56	       <env> L:Int </env>
    57	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    58	       requires FV in_keys(M)
    59	  rule <k> #mkLambda(PNS:ParamNames, CVS:ParamNames, .ParamNames, BODY:Stmts, CM:Map)
    60	        => closureValC(PNS, CVS, BODY, CM) ... </k>
    61	
    62	  // ==== bind params ========================================================
    63	  rule <k> #bindP(.ParamNames, .Vals) => .K ... </k>
    64	  rule <k> #bindP((P:String, PS:ParamNames), (V:Val, VS:Vals)) => #bindP(PS, VS) ... </k>
    65	       <env> L:Int </env>
    66	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ P <- V ], _) ... </scopes>
    67	  // a param that is a cellvar was pre-bound to its cell at frame entry
    68	  rule <k> #bindP((P:String, PS:ParamNames), (V:Val, VS:Vals))
    69	        => #cellW({M[P]}:>Val, V) ~> #bindP(PS, VS) ... </k>
    70	       <env> L:Int </env>
    71	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    72	       requires "$cells" in_keys(M)
    73	        andBool pnMember(P, cellsOf({M["$cells"]}:>Val))
    74	        andBool P in_keys(M) andBool isCellRef({M[P]}:>Val)
    75	       [priority(40)]
    76	
    77	  // ==== return / pop the frame (the returned expr evaluates by strictness) ==
    78	  rule <k> Return(V:Val) ~> _ => #pop </k>
    79	       <ret> noRet => retV(V) </ret>
    80	  rule <k> #endcall => #pop ... </k>
    81	       <ret> noRet => retV(noneV) </ret>
    82	  // pop: restore env, DEALLOCATE the callee frame, and wind scopeLoc back (LIFO allocation
    83	  // makes the saved loc the callee frame's own loc). Sound because no closureVal outlives its
    84	  // defining frame (frontend subset: no returned/stored closures; module defs live in loc 0).
    85	  rule <k> #pop => V ~> CONT </k>
    86	       <ret>   retV(V) => noRet </ret>
    87	       <stack> ListItem(frame(CONT:K, CALLERL:Int, SAVEDL:Int)) => .List ... </stack>
    88	       <env>   L:Int => CALLERL </env>
    89	       <scopes> SC:Map => SC [ L <- undef ] </scopes>
    90	       <scopeLoc> _ => SAVEDL </scopeLoc>
    91	endmodule

    56	        => #bindTgt(T, V) ~> #unpackSeq(TS, VS) ... </k>
    57	  rule <k> #unpackSeq(.Exprs, .ValSeq) => .K ... </k>
    58	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/int.k — MPY-INT
     2	// Int cases of the operator dispatch; Python // and % are floored (pyMod).
     3	
     4	module MPY-INT
     5	  imports MPY-CORE
     6	
     7	  rule applyUn("-", I:Int) => 0 -Int I
     8	
     9	  rule applyBin("+",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 +Int I2
    10	  // Bool participates in int arithmetic (x += (a == b))
    11	  rule applyBin("+",  I:Int, B:Bool) => I +Int #if B #then 1 #else 0 #fi
    12	  rule applyBin("+",  B:Bool, I:Int) => #if B #then 1 #else 0 #fi +Int I
    13	  rule applyBin("-",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 -Int I2
    14	  rule applyBin("*",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 *Int I2
    15	  rule applyBin("%",  I1:Int, I2:Int) => pyMod(I1, I2)
    16	  rule applyBin("//", I1:Int, I2:Int) => (I1 -Int pyMod(I1, I2)) /Int I2
    17	  rule applyBin("**", I1:Int, I2:Int) => I1 ^Int I2 requires I2 >=Int 0
    18	
    19	  syntax Int ::= pyMod(Int, Int) [function]
    20	  rule pyMod(I1:Int, I2:Int) => ((I1 %Int I2) +Int I2) %Int I2
    21	
    22	  rule applyCmp("<",  I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 <Int  I2
    23	  rule applyCmp("<=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 <=Int I2
    24	  rule applyCmp(">",  I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 >Int  I2
    25	  rule applyCmp(">=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 >=Int I2
    26	  rule applyCmp("==", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 ==Int I2
    27	  rule applyCmp("!=", I1:Int, I2:Int)   => I1 =/=Int I2

     1	// reference/src/semantics/operators.k — MPY-OPERATORS
     2	// The operator DISPATCH layer: operands evaluate by strictness (heat/cool over KResult=Val),
     3	// the cooled node hands to applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp (declared in core.k; each domain file
     4	// owns its cases — bool.k, int.k, float.k, str.k, list.k, tuple.k, set.k, dict.k).
     5	
     6	module MPY-OPERATORS
     7	  imports MPY-CORE
     8	  imports MPY-ITER
     9	
    10	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, V:Val) => applyUn(OP, V) ... </k>
    11	
    12	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, R:Val) => applyBin(OP, L, R) ... </k>
    13	
    14	  // Compare's right operand sits under the CmpOp wrapper — contexts instead of attributes
    15	  context Compare(HOLE, _)
    16	  context Compare(_:Val, CmpOp(_, HOLE))
    17	  rule <k> Compare(LV:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, RV:Val)) => applyCmp(OP, LV, RV) ... </k> [owise]
    18	
    19	  rule applyCmp("is",     V:Val, noneV) => V ==K noneV
    20	  rule applyCmp("is not", V:Val, noneV) => notBool (V ==K noneV)
    21	
    22	  // ==== operand deref: heap objects combine/compare by STRUCTURE ============
    23	  // (Python: list == is structural; identity only via `is`.) priority(40)
    24	  // preempts the generic dispatch so applyUn/applyBin/applyCmp never see a ref.
    25	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int), R:Expr) => BinOp(OP, V, R) ... </k>
    26	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    27	       [priority(40)]
    28	  rule <k> BinOp(OP:String, L:Val, ref(H:Int)) => BinOp(OP, L, V) ... </k>
    29	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    30	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    31	       [priority(40)]
    32	
    33	  // the left operand of `in`/`not in` is an ELEMENT (compares by ==K) — never deref'd
    34	  rule <k> Compare(ref(H:Int), CmpOp(OP:String, R:Expr)) => Compare(V, CmpOp(OP, R)) ... </k>
    35	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    36	       requires OP =/=String "in" andBool OP =/=String "not in"
    37	       [priority(40)]
    38	  rule <k> Compare(L:Val, CmpOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int))) => Compare(L, CmpOp(OP, V)) ... </k>
    39	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    40	       requires notBool isRefV(L)
    41	        orBool OP ==String "in" orBool OP ==String "not in"
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	
    44	  rule <k> UnaryOp(OP:String, ref(H:Int)) => UnaryOp(OP, V) ... </k>
    45	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    46	       [priority(40)]
    47	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/bool.k — MPY-BOOL
     2	// Bool operator cases + the truthy boolean operations (not / and / or; and-or are
     3	// value-returning short-circuit over any Vals, per Python).
     4	
     5	module MPY-BOOL
     6	  imports MPY-CORE
     7	
     8	  rule applyUn("not", V:Val) => notBool truthy(V)
     9	
    10	  rule applyCmp("==", B1:Bool, B2:Bool) => B1 ==Bool B2
    11	  rule applyCmp("!=", B1:Bool, B2:Bool) => B1 =/=Bool B2
    12	
    13	  // ==== BoolOp: short-circuit, value-returning and / or =====================
    14	  // the node is its own accumulator: heat the HEAD element only, then either return it
    15	  // (short-circuit) or drop it and continue
    16	  context BoolOp(_, (HOLE:Expr, _:Exprs))
    17	  rule <k> BoolOp(_:String, (V:Val, .Exprs)) => V ... </k>
    18	  rule <k> BoolOp("and", (V:Val, A:Expr, REST:Exprs)) => BoolOp("and", (A, REST)) ... </k>
    19	       requires truthy(V)
    20	  rule <k> BoolOp("and", (V:Val, _:Expr, _:Exprs)) => V ... </k>
    21	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    22	  rule <k> BoolOp("or",  (V:Val, _:Expr, _:Exprs)) => V ... </k>
    23	       requires truthy(V)
    24	  rule <k> BoolOp("or",  (V:Val, A:Expr, REST:Exprs)) => BoolOp("or", (A, REST)) ... </k>
    25	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    26	
    27	  // ==== heap-object head: decide truthiness THROUGH the heap, never rewrite the
    28	  // operand — and/or return the OBJECT itself (Python identity), not its structure
    29	  rule <k> BoolOp(_:String, (ref(H:Int), .Exprs)) => ref(H) ... </k>
    30	       [priority(40)]
    31	  rule <k> BoolOp("and", (ref(H:Int), A:Expr, REST:Exprs)) => BoolOp("and", (A, REST)) ... </k>
    32	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    33	       requires truthy(V)
    34	       [priority(40)]
    35	  rule <k> BoolOp("and", (ref(H:Int), _:Expr, _:Exprs)) => ref(H) ... </k>
    36	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    37	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    38	       [priority(40)]
    39	  rule <k> BoolOp("or", (ref(H:Int), _:Expr, _:Exprs)) => ref(H) ... </k>
    40	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    41	       requires truthy(V)
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	  rule <k> BoolOp("or", (ref(H:Int), A:Expr, REST:Exprs)) => BoolOp("or", (A, REST)) ... </k>
    44	       <heap> ... H |-> V:Val ... </heap>
    45	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    46	       [priority(40)]
    47	endmodule

    12	  // the builtins REGISTRY is core.k's builtinsScope (the -1 frame); names resolve by lookup
    13	
    14	  // Call routing + argument evaluation live in call.k, which also routes the fold
    15	  // builtins (sum/all/any/max/min) to the #_Acc folds below and everything else to
    16	  // applyBuiltin. This module owns applyBuiltin + the fold implementations.

    29	  // Minimal: the "copy a sequence" case (list of a list is itself; list of a tuple keeps order).
    30	  // list() of other iterables (str/range/set/zip) is added via the iterator fold when needed.
    31	  // (k-cell — list() constructs a NEW object)
    32	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("list")), (list(VS:ValSeq),  .Vals)) => #alloc(list(VS)) ... </k>
    33	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("list")), (tuple(VS:ValSeq), .Vals)) => #alloc(list(VS)) ... </k>
    34	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("list")), .Vals)                     => #alloc(list(.ValSeq)) ... </k>

    38	  rule charsOf(iCons(C:Int, R:IntSeq)) => vCons(str(iCons(C, .IntSeq)), charsOf(R))

    42

    44	  rule applyBuiltin("abs", I:Int, .Vals) => absInt(I)
    45	
    46	  // ==== sum(iterable) — one #iterNext fold; intOf = int value of an int/bool ==

    48	  rule <k> #sumAcc(IT:Iterable, ACC:Int) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #sumCont(ACC) ... </k>
    49	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #sumCont(ACC:Int) => ACC ... </k>

    51	        => #sumAcc(R, ACC +Int intOf(V)) ... </k>

    53	
    54	  syntax Int ::= intOf(Val) [function]
    55	  rule intOf(I:Int)  => I
    56	  rule intOf(B:Bool) => #if B #then 1 #else 0 #fi
    57	
    58	  // ==== all / any (short-circuiting #iterNext folds) ========================

    61	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #allCont => true ... </k>
    62	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #allCont => #allAcc(R) ... </k>
    63	       requires truthy(V)
    64	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, _:Iterable) ~> #allCont => false ... </k>
    65	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    66	
    67	  syntax KItem ::= #anyAcc(Iterable) | "#anyCont"
    68	  rule <k> #anyAcc(IT:Iterable) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #anyCont ... </k>
    69	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #anyCont => false ... </k>
    70	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, _:Iterable) ~> #anyCont => true ... </k>
    71	       requires truthy(V)
    72	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #anyCont => #anyAcc(R) ... </k>
    73	       requires notBool truthy(V)
    74	
    75	  // ==== max / min over an iterable (#iterNext folds; first element seeds) ====

    77	  rule <k> #maxAcc0(IT:Iterable) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #maxCont0 ... </k>
    78	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #maxCont0 => #maxAcc(R, {V}:>Int) ... </k>

    80	  rule <k> #maxAcc(IT:Iterable, M:Int) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #maxCont(M) ... </k>
    81	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #maxCont(M:Int) => M ... </k>
    82	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #maxCont(M:Int)
    83	        => #maxAcc(R, maxInt(M, {V}:>Int)) ... </k>

    85	
    86	  syntax KItem ::= #minAcc0(Iterable) | "#minCont0" | #minAcc(Iterable, Int) | #minCont(Int)

    93	        => #minAcc(R, minInt(M, {V}:>Int)) ... </k>

    96	  // ==== variadic max / min (a Vals fold) ====================================

    99	  rule maxVals(M:Int, .Vals)           => M
   100	  rule maxVals(M:Int, (I:Int, R:Vals)) => maxVals(maxInt(M, I), R)
   101	
   102	  syntax Int ::= minVals(Int, Vals) [function]
   103	  rule applyBuiltin("min", I:Int, REST:Vals) => minVals(I, REST)
   104	  rule minVals(M:Int, .Vals)           => M
   105	  rule minVals(M:Int, (I:Int, R:Vals)) => minVals(minInt(M, I), R)

   107	  // ==== bin(n) — "0b" + binary digit codes (promoted from 103's defined fold) ==

   110	  // negative operand: the '-' sign prefixes the magnitude's digits

   112	    => str(iCons(45, iCons(48, iCons(98, binCodes(0 -Int N)))))
   113	       requires N <Int 0
   114	  syntax IntSeq ::= binCodes(Int) [function, total]
   115	  rule binCodes(0) => iCons(48, .IntSeq)
   116	  rule binCodes(N:Int) => binAcc(N, .IntSeq) requires N >Int 0
   117	  syntax IntSeq ::= binAcc(Int, IntSeq) [function, total]

   119	  rule binAcc(N:Int, ACC:IntSeq)
   120	    => binAcc((N -Int pyMod(N, 2)) /Int 2, iCons(48 +Int pyMod(N, 2), ACC))

   123	  // ==== enumerate(xs) — pairs (i, v); materialized eagerly over a list =========

   125	        => #alloc(list(enumVS(VS, 0))) ... </k>

   128	  rule enumVS(vCons(V:Val, R:ValSeq), I:Int)
   129	    => vCons(tuple(vCons(I, vCons(V, .ValSeq))), enumVS(R, I +Int 1))

   139	  // ==== int(x) identities (int(round(x)) composes through) ====================

   155	  // ==== int(str) — a multi-digit non-negative numeral (Horner fold; the single-char rule covers len 1)

   161	
   162	  // ==== zip(a, b) — parallel iterable of pairs, truncating to the shorter =====

   182	  // ==== eval(str) — arithmetic expressions (ints, + - * // **, spaces) ========

   186	  // argument leaves the call unevaluated for problem-level folds.
   187	  rule applyBuiltin("eval", str(CS:IntSeq), .Vals) => evalArith(CS)

   189	  rule evalArith(CS:IntSeq)
   190	    => firstNdE(passAddE(passMulE(passPowE(tokOps(CS), tokNds(CS)))))
   191	
   192	  syntax OpSeq ::= ".OpSeq" | oCons(String, OpSeq)
   193	
   194	  syntax Bool ::= evDigit(Int) [function, total]

   196	  syntax Bool ::= evHead42(IntSeq) [function, total]

   198	  rule evHead42(_:IntSeq)            => false [owise]

   201	  rule evHead47(_:IntSeq)            => false [owise]

   207	  rule tokOps(iCons(42, iCons(42, R:IntSeq))) => oCons("**", tokOps(R))
   208	  rule tokOps(iCons(42, R:IntSeq))     => oCons("*", tokOps(R)) requires notBool evHead42(R)

   210	  rule tokOps(iCons(47, R:IntSeq))     => oCons("/", tokOps(R)) requires notBool evHead47(R)
   211	  rule tokOps(iCons(43, R:IntSeq))     => oCons("+", tokOps(R))
   212	  rule tokOps(iCons(45, R:IntSeq))     => oCons("-", tokOps(R))
   213	
   214	  syntax IntSeq ::= tokNds(IntSeq) [function, total]
   215	                  | tokNdAcc(Int, IntSeq) [function, total]
   216	  rule tokNds(.IntSeq)                => .IntSeq

   167	  syntax Int ::= intPart(IntSeq) [function, total] | intPartAcc(IntSeq, Int) [function, total]

   175	  rule fracPart(iCons(46, R:IntSeq)) => fracAcc(R, 0)

   192	  rule applyBin("/", F:Float, I:Int) => divFloatIntV(F, I)

   195	  syntax Float ::= intToF(Int) [function, total, symbol(intToF), no-evaluators]
   196	  rule intToF(I:Int) => Int2Float(I, 53, 11) [concrete]
   197	  rule applyBin("+", I:Int, F:Float) => addF(intToF(I), F)
   198	  rule applyBin("+", F:Float, I:Int) => addF(F, intToF(I))
   199	  rule applyBin("-", I:Int, F:Float) => subF(intToF(I), F)
   200	  rule applyBin("-", F:Float, I:Int) => subF(F, intToF(I))

   202	  rule applyBin("*", F:Float, I:Int) => mulF(F, intToF(I))

   204	  rule applyCmp("<", F:Float, I:Int) => floatLt(F, intToF(I))
   205	  rule applyCmp(">", I:Int, F:Float) => gtF(intToF(I), F)
   206	  rule applyCmp(">", F:Float, I:Int) => gtF(F, intToF(I))

   211	  rule applyBuiltin("int", F:Float, .Vals) => truncF(F)
   212	
   213	  rule applyBuiltin("float", I:Int, .Vals)   => intToF(I)
   214	  rule applyBuiltin("float", F:Float, .Vals) => F

   216	  // round: Python half-even (banker's); round(F, N) scales by 10^N

   218	  rule roundF(F:Float)
   219	    => #if (F -Float floorFloat(F)) ==Float 0.5
   220	       #then (#if Float2Int(floorFloat(F)) %Int 2 ==Int 0
   221	              #then Float2Int(floorFloat(F)) #else Float2Int(ceilFloat(F)) #fi)
   222	       #else Float2Int(floorFloat(F +Float 0.5)) #fi [concrete]
   223	  syntax Float ::= roundFN(Float, Int) [function, total, symbol(roundFN), no-evaluators]

   226	       /Float Int2Float(10 ^Int N, 53, 11) [concrete]
   227	  rule applyBuiltin("round", F:Float, .Vals)        => roundF(F)
   228	  rule applyBuiltin("round", F:Float, N:Int, .Vals) => roundFN(F, N)
   229	
   230	  syntax Float ::= sqrtF(Float) [function, total, symbol(sqrtF), no-evaluators]
   231	  rule sqrtF(F:Float) => sqrtFloat(F) [concrete]
   232	  syntax KItem ::= "#mathSqrt"
   233	  rule <k> Call(Attribute(Name("math"), "sqrt"), (E:Expr, .Exprs)) => E ~> #mathSqrt ... </k> [priority(40)]
   234	  rule <k> F:Float ~> #mathSqrt => sqrtF(F) ... </k>
   235	  rule <k> I:Int ~> #mathSqrt => sqrtF(intToF(I)) ... </k>
   236	
   237	  // ---- min / max over a FLOAT list — FLOAT branch of the shared #minCont0/#maxCont0 folds (which
   238	  // seed/step with `requires isInt(V)`, so they are STUCK on floats). These add the `requires
   239	  // isFloat(V)` seed + a Float-accumulator fold via K's minFloat/maxFloat — concrete for krun. A proof
   240	  // over a SYMBOLIC float list intercepts min/max problem-locally to an opaque minVF/maxVF (at
   241	  // #applyK, priority 40, in its verification.k) BEFORE #minAcc0, so this fold is krun-only. Additive:
   242	  // the isFloat guard is disjoint from the existing isInt one.
   243	  syntax KItem ::= #maxAccF(Iterable, Float) | #maxContF(Float)
   244	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #maxCont0 => #maxAccF(R, {V}:>Float) ... </k> requires isFloat(V)
   245	  rule <k> #maxAccF(IT:Iterable, M:Float) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #maxContF(M) ... </k>
   246	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #maxContF(M:Float) => M ... </k>
   247	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #maxContF(M:Float) => #maxAccF(R, maxFloat(M, {V}:>Float)) ... </k>
   248	       requires isFloat(V)
   249	
   250	  syntax KItem ::= #minAccF(Iterable, Float) | #minContF(Float)
   251	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #minCont0 => #minAccF(R, {V}:>Float) ... </k> requires isFloat(V)
   252	  rule <k> #minAccF(IT:Iterable, M:Float) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #minContF(M) ... </k>
   253	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #minContF(M:Float) => M ... </k>
   254	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #minContF(M:Float) => #minAccF(R, minFloat(M, {V}:>Float)) ... </k>
   255	       requires isFloat(V)
   256	
   257	  // ---- sum over a float list (krun; mirrors the min/max float paths). The Int-only shared
   258	  // #sumCont sticks on a Float yield; switch to a Float-headed fold via addF (concrete twin).
   259	  // The switch guard carries the SYNTACTIC negation of the Int rule's guard so a symbolic proof
   260	  // with isInt(V) in its path condition refutes this branch without sort reasoning.
   261	  syntax KItem ::= #sumAccF(Iterable, Float) | #sumContF(Float)
   262	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #sumCont(ACC:Int)
   263	        => #sumAccF(R, addF(intToF(ACC), {V}:>Float)) ... </k>
   264	       requires isFloat(V) andBool notBool (isInt(V) orBool isBool(V))
   265	  rule <k> #sumAccF(IT:Iterable, ACC:Float) => #iterNext(IT) ~> #sumContF(ACC) ... </k>
   266	  rule <k> #iterDone ~> #sumContF(ACC:Float) => ACC ... </k>
   267	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #sumContF(ACC:Float)
   268	        => #sumAccF(R, addF(ACC, {V}:>Float)) ... </k>
   269	       requires isFloat(V)
   270	  rule <k> #iterYield(V:Val, R:Iterable) ~> #sumContF(ACC:Float)
   271	        => #sumAccF(R, addF(ACC, intToF(intOf(V)))) ... </k>
   272	       requires isInt(V) orBool isBool(V)
   273	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/dict.k — MPY-DICT
     2	//
     3	// Minimal dict support. A dict value is `dictV(KS, VS)`: PARALLEL insertion-ordered key/value
     4	// ValSeqs (Python dict order; keys distinct; re-inserting a key updates its value in place, keeping
     5	// the original position). Concrete for krun (the ordered build + `.keys()` are the real ops); a proof
     6	// over a SYMBOLIC dict passes `dictV(KS, WS)` with a symbolic key sequence KS and reads
     7	// `d.keys() = list(KS)`, then keeps each key opaque problem-locally.
     8	//
     9	// Only the pieces needed so far: a dict VALUE (so `{}` inside a mixed list evaluates and
    10	// `isinstance(x, int)` rejects it), the `{k: v, ...}` literal, and `.keys()`. More dict ops (subscript
    11	// / `.get()` / `.values()` / dict `==`) are added as dict problems need them — kept minimal + additive.
    12	
    13	module MPY-DICT
    14	  imports MPY-CORE
    15	  imports MPY-ITER
    16	  imports MPY-METHODS
    17	  imports MPY-LIST
    18	
    19	  // dict as PARALLEL ordered key/value ValSeqs (same length; keys distinct).
    20	  syntax Val ::= dictV(ValSeq, ValSeq)
    21	
    22	  // ==== DictExpr: {k: v, ...} literal. Eval each key then value, left to right, insert-with-dedup.
    23	  syntax KItem ::= #dictAcc(Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    24	                 | #dictKey(Expr, Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    25	                 | #dictVal(Val, Entries, ValSeq, ValSeq)
    26	  rule <k> DictExpr(ES:Entries) => #dictAcc(ES, .ValSeq, .ValSeq) ... </k>
    27	  rule <k> #dictAcc(.Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq) => dictV(KS, VS) ... </k>
    28	  rule <k> #dictAcc((Entry(K:Expr, V:Expr), REST:Entries), KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    29	        => K ~> #dictKey(V, REST, KS, VS) ... </k>
    30	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dictKey(V:Expr, REST:Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    31	        => V ~> #dictVal(KV, REST, KS, VS) ... </k>
    32	  rule <k> VV:Val ~> #dictVal(KV:Val, REST:Entries, KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq)
    33	        => #dictAcc(REST, dPutK(KS, KV), dPutV(KS, VS, KV, VV)) ... </k>
    34	
    35	  // insert-with-dedup helpers (concrete Val key equality via ==K). [total] so buildFold over a dict is
    36	  // total (its #Ceil is #Top) — needed when a symbolic proof carries a built dict as a config value.
    37	  syntax Bool ::= dHasKey(ValSeq, Val) [function, total]
    38	  rule dHasKey(.ValSeq, _:Val)                => false
    39	  rule dHasKey(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), K:Val) => true          requires A ==K K
    40	  rule dHasKey(vCons(A:Val, R:ValSeq), K:Val) => dHasKey(R, K) requires notBool (A ==K K)
    41	
    42	  // dPutK: KS unchanged if K already present, else append K (keep-first-position).
    43	  syntax ValSeq ::= dPutK(ValSeq, Val) [function, total]
    44	  rule dPutK(KS:ValSeq, K:Val) => KS                                  requires dHasKey(KS, K)
    45	  rule dPutK(KS:ValSeq, K:Val) => valSeqConcat(KS, vCons(K, .ValSeq)) requires notBool dHasKey(KS, K)
    46	
    47	  // dPutV: parallel to KS — set the value at K's position if present, else append V at the end. The
    48	  // [owise] catch-all covers the degenerate mismatched-length case (never reached for a well-formed dict).
    49	  syntax ValSeq ::= dPutV(ValSeq, ValSeq, Val, Val) [function, total]
    50	  rule dPutV(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), vCons(_:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val)  => vCons(V, VR)
    51	       requires A ==K K
    52	  rule dPutV(vCons(A:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val) => vCons(B, dPutV(KR, VR, K, V))
    53	       requires notBool (A ==K K)
    54	  rule dPutV(_KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq, _K:Val, V:Val) => valSeqConcat(VS, vCons(V, .ValSeq)) [owise]
    55	
    56	  // ==== dict methods ========================================================
    57	  // d.keys() -> a FRESH list object of the ordered keys (k-cell: it allocates).
    58	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(dictV(KS:ValSeq, _:ValSeq), "keys")), .Vals)
    59	        => #alloc(list(KS)) ... </k>
    60	       [priority(40)]
    61	
    62	  // ==== dict subscript READ: d[k] (assoc lookup; KeyError is out of subset) ==
    63	  rule applyIndexD(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val) => dGet(KS, VS, K)
    64	  syntax Val ::= applyIndexD(Val, Val) [function]
    65	  rule <k> Subscript(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val) => applyIndexD(dictV(KS, VS), K) ... </k>
    66	       [priority(45)]
    67	
    68	  // ==== dict subscript-assign: d[k] = v (insert/update in place) =============
    69	  // Only for a LOCAL dict variable X (the current scope holds it). Reuses dPutK/dPutV.
    70	  syntax Val ::= dictSet(Val, Val, Val) [function]
    71	  rule dictSet(dictV(KS:ValSeq, VS:ValSeq), K:Val, V:Val) => dictV(dPutK(KS, K), dPutV(KS, VS, K, V))
    72	
    73	  // RHS evaluates first (Assign strictness), then the key. Dispatch on the scope
    74	  // value: a bare dict updates in the scope (dicts stay values); a ref (a heap
    75	  // list — or a heap dict later) writes the heap in place.
    76	  syntax KItem ::= #dsetK(String, Val)
    77	  rule <k> Assign(Subscript(Name(X:String), K:Expr), VV:Val) => K ~> #dsetK(X, VV) ... </k>
    78	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dsetK(X:String, VV:Val) => .K ... </k>
    79	       <env> L:Int </env>
    80	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map => M [ X <- dictSet({M[X]}:>Val, KV, VV) ], _) ... </scopes>
    81	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool notBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    82	  rule <k> KV:Val ~> #dsetK(X:String, VV:Val) => #dsetV({M[X]}:>Val, KV, VV) ... </k>
    83	       <env> L:Int </env>
    84	       <scopes> ... L |-> scope(M:Map, _) ... </scopes>
    85	       requires X in_keys(M) andBool isRefV({M[X]}:>Val)
    86	  syntax KItem ::= #dsetV(Val, Val, Val)
    87	  rule <k> #dsetV(ref(H:Int), I:Int, VV:Val) => .K ... </k>
    88	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => setVSAt(VS, normIdxD(I, vsLen(VS)), VV)) ... </heap>
    89	  // negative-index normalization local to the write (subscript.k's is not imported here)
    90	  syntax Int ::= normIdxD(Int, Int) [function, total]
    91	  rule normIdxD(I:Int, LEN:Int) => I +Int LEN requires I  <Int 0
    92	  rule normIdxD(I:Int, _:Int)   => I          requires I >=Int 0
    93	
    94	  // ==== dict == (order-insensitive: same size + same key->value pairs) =======
    95	  rule applyCmp("==", dictV(KS1:ValSeq, VS1:ValSeq), dictV(KS2:ValSeq, VS2:ValSeq))
    96	    => (vsLen(KS1) ==Int vsLen(KS2)) andBool dSubset(KS1, VS1, KS2, VS2)
    97	  syntax Bool ::= dSubset(ValSeq, ValSeq, ValSeq, ValSeq) [function]
    98	  rule dSubset(.ValSeq, .ValSeq, _:ValSeq, _:ValSeq) => true
    99	  rule dSubset(vCons(K:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(V:Val, VR:ValSeq), KS2:ValSeq, VS2:ValSeq)
   100	    => dHasKey(KS2, K) andBool (dGet(KS2, VS2, K) ==K V) andBool dSubset(KR, VR, KS2, VS2)
   101	  syntax Val ::= dGet(ValSeq, ValSeq, Val) [function]
   102	  rule dGet(vCons(A:Val, _:ValSeq), vCons(B:Val, _:ValSeq), K:Val) => B                requires A ==K K
   103	  rule dGet(vCons(A:Val, KR:ValSeq), vCons(_:Val, VR:ValSeq), K:Val) => dGet(KR, VR, K) requires notBool (A ==K K)
   104	endmodule
     1	// reference/src/semantics/sort.k — MPY-SORT
     2	// Trusted sorted(): sorted(list) as an opaque ascending permutation `sortVS` — opaque symbolic
     3	// for kprove (a trusted primitive, correctness/ordering proved in Lean / notes/sort-probe),
     4	// and a concrete insertion sort for krun. Wrappers verify the logic AROUND the sort (index /
     5	// slice / filter / dedup); indexing an opaque sortVS(VS) carries through as an opaque term, so
     6	// no ordering lemma is needed in K — the trust (sortVS = real sorted) is discharged by each
     7	// problem's differential test. Only int lists (compared by projectIntTotal); keyed / string
     8	// sorts are separate. Fires only via the "sorted" builtin, so inert for non-sorting programs.
     9	
    10	module MPY-SORT
    11	  imports MPY-BUILTINS
    12	  imports MPY-SUBSCRIPT
    13	
    14	  // sortVS(VS): the ascending sort of the Val list VS. Opaque for symbolic VS (no-evaluators);
    15	  // concrete insertion sort for krun.
    16	  // Concrete sort matches Int-sorted elements directly (an int Val IS an Int); projectIntTotal
    17	  // (lemmas-only) is not available in the semantics. Int and str lists.
    18	  syntax ValSeq ::= sortVS(ValSeq) [function, total, symbol(sortVS), no-evaluators]
    19	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVS(Int, ValSeq) [function]
    20	  rule sortVS(.ValSeq)                => .ValSeq          [concrete]
    21	  rule sortVS(vCons(X:Int, R:ValSeq)) => insVS(X, sortVS(R)) [concrete]
    22	  rule insVS(X:Int, .ValSeq)                => vCons(X, .ValSeq) [concrete]
    23	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Int, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(X, vCons(Y, R)) requires X <=Int Y [concrete]
    24	  rule insVS(X:Int, vCons(Y:Int, R:ValSeq)) => vCons(Y, insVS(X, R)) requires X  >Int Y [concrete]
    25	  // str elements insert by the shared lexicographic strLt (methods.k)
    26	  syntax ValSeq ::= insVSs(IntSeq, ValSeq) [function]
    27	  rule sortVS(vCons(str(CS:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => insVSs(CS, sortVS(R)) [concrete]
    28	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, .ValSeq) => vCons(str(A), .ValSeq) [concrete]
    29	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(A), vCons(str(B), R))
    30	       requires strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B [concrete]
    31	  rule insVSs(A:IntSeq, vCons(str(B:IntSeq), R:ValSeq)) => vCons(str(B), insVSs(A, R))
    32	       requires notBool (strLt(A, B) orBool A ==K B) [concrete]
    33	
    34	  // sorted(list) constructs a NEW object: k-cell pre-dispatch (beats the [owise]
    35	  // applyBuiltin routing in call.k) so the result allocates.
    36	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(builtinV("sorted")), (list(VS:ValSeq), .Vals))
    37	        => #alloc(list(sortVS(VS))) ... </k>
    38	
    39	  // mutator: xs.sort() — the in-place heap write over the same trusted sortVS
    40	  rule <k> #applyK(toCall(boundMethodV(ref(H:Int), "sort")), .Vals) => noneV ... </k>
    41	       <heap> ... H |-> list(VS:ValSeq => sortVS(VS)) ... </heap>
    42	       [priority(40)]
    43	
    44	  // ==== keyed / reversed sorted() (WP2) =====================================
    45	  // sortKeyVS(VS, KV): the stable ascending sort of VS by the key value KV
    46	  // (a closure/builtin/type — anything callable). OPAQUE here; the concrete
    47	  // leg (MPY-CONCRETE, llvm only) computes keys by REAL calls and stable-
    48	  // inserts, at priority(40) over these.
    49	  syntax ValSeq ::= sortKeyVS(ValSeq, Val) [function, total, symbol(sortKeyVS), no-evaluators]
    50

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Line-addressed inventory of K declarations, rules, claims, and attributes."""

from __future__ import annotations

import collections
import re
from pathlib import Path


ROOT = Path("/tmp/audit-work/152-compare/candidate")
files = sorted((ROOT / "reference-semantics").rglob("*.k"))
files.extend(
    [
        ROOT / "verification.k",
        ROOT / "spec.k",
        ROOT / "operational-spec.k",
        ROOT / "mutation-spec.k",
    ]
)

directive = re.compile(
    r"^\s*(requires|module|imports|configuration|syntax|context|rule|claim)\b"
)
attribute_words = (
    "function",
    "functional",
    "total",
    "macro",
    "macro-rec",
    "no-evaluators",
    "concrete",
    "priority",
    "owise",
    "strict",
    "seqstrict",
)

grand_counts: collections.Counter[str] = collections.Counter()
print("K_RULE_INVENTORY")
for path in files:
    relative = path.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix()
    counts: collections.Counter[str] = collections.Counter()
    entries: list[tuple[int, str, str]] = []
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
        for line_number, raw_line in enumerate(stream, 1):
            line = raw_line.rstrip()
            match = directive.match(line)
            if match:
                kind = match.group(1)
                counts[kind] += 1
                grand_counts[kind] += 1
                entries.append((line_number, kind, line.strip()))
            if any(f"[{word}" in line or f", {word}" in line for word in attribute_words):
                for word in attribute_words:
                    if re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(word)}\b", line):
                        counts[f"attr:{word}"] += 1
                        grand_counts[f"attr:{word}"] += 1
    print(f"FILE {relative}")
    print(f"COUNTS {dict(sorted(counts.items()))}")
    for line_number, kind, text in entries:
        print(f"  {line_number:04d} {kind:13s} {text}")

print(f"GRAND_COUNTS {dict(sorted(grand_counts.items()))}")

(`evidence/03_build_verification.log`, `evidence/03_kprove_spec.log`).

Bridge-free finite proof:

```sh
kompile verification.k \
  --backend haskell \
  --main-module COMPARE-COMMON \
  --syntax-module MPY-SYNTAX \
  --output-definition audit-operational-kompiled

kprove operational-spec.k \
  --definition audit-operational-kompiled \
  --spec-module COMPARE-OPERATIONAL-SPEC
```

Both exited 0; `kprove` printed `#Top`
(`evidence/03_build_operational.log`,
`evidence/03_kprove_operational.log`).

The LLVM build emitted non-exhaustiveness warnings for helpers belonging to
unused map/float/string/subscript features. The Haskell builds emitted only
unused-variable warnings in two string-comparison rules. None prevented a build
or matched the submitted program. These clean `#Top` results establish closure
under the compiled theory; Stage 5 shows that the bridge-enabled theory is
unsound.

## 4. Adequacy and real-program pinning

### Entry claims

The three claims in `/candidate/spec.k` share the standard initial state:
module scope 0 is empty with parent builtins scope -1, `scopeLoc=1`, the heap is
empty with `heapLoc=0`, the call stack is empty, and return/exception states are
`noRet`/`NoExc`. They have no unsatisfiable side condition.

1. The universal claim defines `compare`, calls it with
   `list(intVals(GAME))` and `list(intVals(GUESS))` for arbitrary finite
   `IntSeq` values, and requires returned value `ref(0)`. It requires heap
   location 0 to contain
   `list(absDiffs(intVals(GAME), intVals(GUESS)))`, `heapLoc=1`, the exact
   global closure, an empty stack, and no exception.
2. The first example claim requires the exact first prompt output
   `[0,0,0,0,3,3]`.
3. The second example claim requires the exact second prompt output
   `[4,4,1,0,0,6]`.

The universal formal domain includes unequal lengths and gives zip truncation;
therefore it covers, rather than narrows, all equal-length integer-list cases.
The result is not free or tautological: both the returned ref and its exact heap
contents are constrained.

The four entry claims in `/candidate/operational-spec.k` import
`COMPARE-COMMON`, excluding the loop bridge. They prove the two examples,
empty/empty returning empty, and `[-7,9]` versus `[5,-4]` returning `[12,13]`.
They are meaningful finite execution claims, not an arbitrary-length theorem.
There is no helper or loop reachability claim connecting the fixed loop to
`absDiffs`.

### Mechanical program identity

Using the fresh proof definition, `kast --expand-macros` parsed both the trusted
fresh `solution.mpy` and the claim's `compareDef`. The reviewer script unwraps
the sole function statement from the translated `Module` and compares the KAST
JSON recursively:

```sh
kast solution.mpy --definition audit-verification-kompiled \
  --expand-macros --output json --output-file solution.kast.json
kast --expression 'compareDef' --sort Stmt --module COMPARE-COMMON \
  --definition audit-verification-kompiled --expand-macros \
  --output json --output-file compareDef.kast.json
python3 /audit-output/evidence/04_constructor_pinning.py
```

All exited 0; `constructor_terms_equal=True`
(`evidence/04_kast_expansion.log`,
`evidence/04_constructor_pinning.log`). Thus the claim executes the exact
submitted function binding and body, not a substituted program.

A concrete satisfying instance is `GAME=[1,-2,3]` and
`GUESS=[4,-2,-5]`. `absDiffs`, the trusted canonical, and generated Python all
give `[3,0,8]` (`evidence/04_ground_witness.log`).

Stage 4 therefore passes program identity, precondition satisfiability, and
result constraint. These facts do not validate a proof-local rule that replaces
the pinned body's execution.

## 5. Rule-by-rule static soundness review

The complete line-addressed inventory is
`evidence/05_inventory.log`; the per-file/per-extension decision ledger is
`evidence/05_rule_assessment.md`. It covers all 232 syntax declarations, 704
rule starts, the configuration, five contexts, imports, claims, attributes,
priority rules, functions, total declarations, macros, and opaque symbols in
the supplied tree plus candidate proof/spec files. There are no
`[functional]` or simplification declarations.

The actual source path is:

```text
Module/load → FuncDef/closure → Call/frame/parameter binding
→ docstring/Expr discard → empty ListExpr/allocation → Assign(result)
→ lookup/call zip → For/#loop → zip #iterNext
→ tuple target binding(score,prediction)
→ integer subtraction → builtin abs → bound append/heap update
→ loop recurrence → Return(result)/frame pop
```

The supplied rules preserve that evaluation order and all relevant cells.
They use mathematical K integers, zip truncation, and fresh heap allocation.
The 25 opaque or concrete-only symbols in the full supplied semantics are
`floorFI`, `toF`, `ceilF`, `intFloatDiv`, `divII`, `floatMod`, `floatLt`,
`absF`, `subF`, `divF`, `addF`, `mulF`, `powF`, `gtF`, `eqF`, `decStrToF`,
`divFloatIntV`, `intToF`, `truncF`, `roundF`, `roundFN`, `sqrtF`,
`md5hexCodes`, `sortVS`, and `sortKeyVS`. None occurs on a target proof path.

Candidate-local extensions:

- `intVals` has disjoint empty/cons equations, justified totality, and
  structural descent.
- `absDiffs` has disjoint empty-left, empty-right, and both-nonempty equations;
  on every claim use it is a terminating definition of zip-truncated
  elementwise `absInt(A-B)`.
- `appendBody`, `compareBody`, and `compareDef` are exact syntax macros, as
  confirmed by the constructor comparison.
- `/candidate/verification.k:50-67` is a priority-40 operational bridge:

  ```k
  #loop(zipObj(GAME, GUESS), TupleExpr(...), appendBody) => .K ...
  ```

  It directly changes the result heap entry to
  `valSeqConcat(ACC, absDiffs(GAME, GUESS))`.

The last rule is materially unsound. It preempts fixed
`controls.k:71` execution and skips iterator steps, tuple assignments,
subtraction, builtin dispatch, append calls, and loop control. Its `...` in the
`<k>` cell admits every trailing continuation, but it neither writes
`score`/`prediction` nor restricts the continuation from observing them. Its
guard checks only that `result` maps to the updated heap reference. No
bridge-free universal connection theorem exists, and the finite claims in
`operational-spec.k` cannot supply one.

### Concrete false-conclusion witness

`evidence/05_bridge_context_spec.k` starts from the same one-pair integer loop:

- `GAME=[1]`, `GUESS=[2]`;
- `result` points to an empty list;
- the pre-loop bindings are `score=99`, `prediction=88`;
- immediately after the loop, the continuation evaluates `Name("score")`.

Fixed execution binds `score=1` and `prediction=2`, appends `1`, and produces
`1`. The bridge appends `1` but skips both bindings, so the continuation
produces stale `99`.

```sh
kprove 05_bridge_context_spec.k \
  --definition audit-verification-kompiled \
  --spec-module BRIDGE-CONTEXT-FALSE
```

Exit 0, `#Top`: the bridge-enabled theory proves the false `99` conclusion
(`evidence/05_bridge_false_proves.log`).

```sh
kprove 05_bridge_context_spec.k \
  --definition audit-operational-kompiled \
  --spec-module FIXED-CONTEXT-REJECT-FALSE
```

Exit 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState`. The residual explicitly contains `<k> 1`,
`score |-> 1`, `prediction |-> 2`, and result list `[1]`
(`evidence/05_fixed_false_rejected.log`).

```sh
kprove 05_bridge_context_spec.k \
  --definition audit-operational-kompiled \
  --spec-module FIXED-CONTEXT-CORRECT
```

Exit 0, `#Top` (`evidence/05_fixed_correct_proves.log`).

This is a satisfiable false-conclusion witness over integer lists inside the
bridge's complete declared match domain. It specifically demonstrates the
context/state mismatch rather than merely asserting a missing proof.

Finally, the universal claim was copied unchanged except for importing
`COMPARE-COMMON`, removing the bridge:

```sh
kprove 05_universal_without_bridge.k \
  --definition audit-operational-kompiled \
  --spec-module UNIVERSAL-WITHOUT-BRIDGE \
  --depth 100
```

Exit 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState` and two unexplored symbolic branches
(`evidence/05_universal_without_bridge_depth100.log`). This bounded diagnostic
does not show that the desired theorem is false; it confirms that the delivered
universal `#Top` depends on the rejected extension and that no legitimate
universal proof remains after its removal.

## 6. Fresh non-vacuity test

I did not rely on `/candidate/mutation-spec.k`. The fresh
`evidence/06_false_result_spec.k` executes the exact `compareDef` on satisfying
input `([1],[2])` but changes only the result-bearing heap postcondition from
the true `[1]` to false `[2]`.

The mutation first built successfully:

```sh
kprove 06_false_result_spec.k \
  --definition audit-verification-kompiled \
  --spec-module AUDITOR-FALSE-RESULT-SPEC \
  --dry-run
```

Exit 0 (`evidence/06_false_result_dry_run.log`).

The actual proof command was:

```sh
kprove 06_false_result_spec.k \
  --definition audit-verification-kompiled \
  --spec-module AUDITOR-FALSE-RESULT-SPEC
```

Exit 1 with `WarnStuckClaimState`. The residual is the expected normal return
`ref(0)` with heap location 0 containing `[1]`, directly exposing the unmet
`[2]` result obligation (`evidence/06_false_result_rejected.log`). This is a
valid non-vacuity result. It shows that the final claim constrains its answer;
it does not cure the independent operational-rule unsoundness.

## 7. Proven versus assumed accounting

### What the successful K runs establish

Under the **extended candidate theory**, the universal `#Top` establishes
partial correctness of the formal entry claim for arbitrary finite integer
sequences: the exact translated binding/body reaches a returned fresh list
whose symbolic contents are `absDiffs`, with the specified final scope, heap,
stack, return, and exception cells. The two examples close in that same theory.

Under the **fixed supplied theory without the bridge**, four concrete entry
claims close: the two examples, empty input, and one additional two-element
case. Those are legitimate finite reachability facts only.

Because the extended theory contains the demonstrated false transition, its
universal `#Top` proves closure under an unsound rewrite system, not the
requested theorem about fixed execution of the real program.

### Trust ledger

| Boundary | Influence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Trusted supplied semantics, byte-identical candidate copy | Defines all source execution, state, calls, and control | Accepted as the selected semantics boundary; relevant rules were also statically reviewed and concretely exercised. |
| K 7.1.293 compiler/prover and Haskell/LLVM backends | Builds and checks all K artifacts | Ordinary toolchain trust. Fresh builds avoid candidate binaries/caches. |
| K integer/Boolean/string/map/list hooks, especially `-Int` and `absInt` | Directly determines numeric results and state representation | Accepted low-level mathematical/runtime primitive boundary. |
| The 25 supplied opaque/concrete-only symbols listed in Stage 5 | Potentially affect floats, sorting, MD5, and conversions | Accepted but irrelevant here: none appears on a target path or in a postcondition. |
| `intVals` and `absDiffs` equations | Encode formal inputs and mathematical expected result | Equations themselves are truthful and terminating on every use. |
| Priority-40 candidate loop bridge | Determines universal loop result and control/state transition | Illegitimate. It is program-derived, lacks a bridge-free universal connection theorem, admits a broader continuation than any justification, and enables the concrete false conclusion in Stage 5. |
| Mechanical KAST comparison | Connects trusted translation to claim macro | Strong identity evidence; it does not establish semantic correctness of the bridge. |
| Python differential test | Connects generated Python behavior to trusted canonical behavior on 408,913 inputs | Finite empirical support only; not a K proof or a universal connection theorem. |
| LLVM concrete harness and bridge-free finite K claims | Exercise fixed execution on normal/boundary cases | Finite operational evidence only. |
| Informal observation that the submitted suffix returns only `result` | Suggests skipped loop-variable bindings are unobserved in this one body | Insufficient: the actual bridge rule accepts arbitrary suffixes and is globally false on its match domain. Priority does not narrow that domain. |

### Decision

Stages 1-4 reconstruct authentic inputs, a correct implementation, clean
positive `#Top` runs, a pinned program term, satisfiable preconditions, and a
result-constraining postcondition. Stage 6 confirms non-vacuity. Stage 5 is
fatal: the universal proof relies on a materially unsound operational bridge,
and a machine-checked witness shows the exact false conclusion it enables. The
bridge-free finite claims and differential tests cannot substitute for the
missing universal fixed-semantics connection proof.
